note: Canonical cross-language concept vocabulary for the Human Languages curriculum. See code/specs/HL01-concept-taxonomy-and-data-layer.md. Ids are stable slugs (never renumbered). 'core: true' = expected in every track once it declares parity:complete. 'retires' lists the pre-canonical concept_tags this id replaced during the HL01 normalization, kept for traceability.

GREETING-HELLO.notes: The default meeting greeting. Where a track taught two 'hello' words, the more formal/ceremonial one moves to GREETING-FORMAL (avē, namaskāraḥ, sat srī akāl).

GREETING-DAY.notes: bonjour / Guten Tag / buongiorno / bom dia. Distinct from GREETING-MORNING and from the noun TIME-DAY.

GREETING-GOODNIGHT.gloss: good night (said on parting / before sleep)
GREETING-GOODNIGHT.notes: Parting greeting, distinct from the meeting greeting GREETING-EVENING. Retires Spanish/Italian's older GREETING-NIGHT tag; where a track's 'noches/notte' word doubles as the evening noun, the noun is TIME-NIGHT.

GREETING-FORMAL.notes: as-salāmu ʿalaykum, namaskār/namaskāra, avē, sat srī akāl. The formal counterpart to GREETING-HELLO within a track.

FAREWELL.notes: Unifies the parting word across tracks (valē, āshi, alvidā, येतो/येते). The plain goodbye (adiós, au revoir, auf Wiedersehen); the time-specific 'see you …' partings are FAREWELL-LATER/TOMORROW/SOON.

FAREWELL-LATER.notes: hasta luego / à bientôt / bis später / a più tardi / até logo. Distinct from the plain FAREWELL.

FAREWELL-TOMORROW.notes: hasta mañana / à demain / bis morgen / a domani / até amanhã.

FAREWELL-SOON.notes: hasta pronto / à bientôt / bis bald / a presto / até breve.

FAREWELL-CASUAL.notes: The informal parting distinct from the neutral FAREWELL: German tschüss, French salut/tchao, Italian ciao, Portuguese tchau.

COURTESY-THANKS.notes: The default 'thank you'. Where a track teaches a second, more colloquial word (often Perso-Arabic), that one is COURTESY-THANKS-CASUAL.

COURTESY-THANKS-CASUAL.notes: e.g. Hindi shukriyā, Punjabi shukrīā — the everyday, often Perso-Arabic-derived alternative to the Sanskritic COURTESY-THANKS.

COURTESY-PLEASE.notes: Requesting-a-favour formula: Russian пожалуйста, French s'il vous plaît, Spanish por favor, German bitte. Several languages (Russian, German) use the same word to reply to thanks.

RESPONSE-YES.notes: Tracks that teach yes and no in a single lesson use RESPONSE-YESNO until that lesson is split during the parity pass.

RESPONSE-YESNO.gloss: yes / no (taught together in one lesson)
RESPONSE-YESNO.notes: A single lesson realizing both yes and no (ita/nōn, hāṇ/nahīṇ, hyã/nā, ām/na). Split into RESPONSE-YES + RESPONSE-NO when the track reaches parity.

INTRO-NICE-TO-MEET-YOU.notes: Some tracks realize this with a bare 'joy/happiness' noun (khushī, magizhchi, santōṣa); that word is the realization.

GRAMMAR-THE.notes: One join key for 'the'; the realization holds each language's specific forms (el/la, der/die/das, il/la/lo, o/a, al-).

COURTESY-YOUREWELCOME.gloss: you're welcome (the standard reply to thanks)
COURTESY-YOUREWELCOME.notes: The reply that closes a thanks exchange (de nada, prego, bitte, не за что). Distinct from GREETING-WELCOME (svāgatam), which welcomes an arrival.

STATE-HOW-ARE-YOU.gloss: how are you? (asking after someone's state)
STATE-HOW-ARE-YOU.notes: The realization holds each language's phrasing and register split (¿cómo está usted? / ¿cómo estás?). Builds on QUESTION-HOW plus the state verb.

WORD-SOSO.gloss: so-so / not bad (a middling answer to 'how are you?')
WORD-SOSO.notes: The neither-good-nor-bad reply (regular / más o menos, così così, comme ci comme ça).

namespaced.note: Language-local lexical/structural concepts do NOT appear here; they live only in lesson frontmatter as <LANG>-<NAME> (pattern ^[A-Z]{2}-[A-Z0-9-]+$). Current examples, for reference:

examples.ES-SE-LLAMA: se llama — 'he/she calls himself' (3rd-person of llamar)
examples.ES-WORD-HASTA: hasta — 'until / up to' (← Arabic ḥattā; a rare borrowed function word)
examples.ES-VERB-ESTAR: estar — 'to be' (temporary state / location; ← Latin stare 'to stand')
examples.IT-VERB-STARE: stare — 'to be' (state; ← Latin stare 'to stand', = Spanish estar); drives 'come stai?'
examples.FR-VERB-ALLER: aller — 'to go' (suppletive: ambulāre/vādere/īre); drives 'comment ça va?'
examples.DE-VERB-GEHEN: gehen — 'to go' (= English go); drives 'wie geht es dir?'
examples.PT-WORD-TUDO: tudo — 'everything / all' (← Latin tōtus); the heart of 'tudo bem?'

practiceTags.note: Non-word lessons (type: review | practice-mix | writing) carry a session/orthography label, not a concept, and are exempt from the cross-language join. Existing labels: CH1-PRACTICE, CH2-PRACTICE, CH3-PRACTICE, CH4-PRACTICE, REVIEW.
